Overview & Purpose of the Factories Act 1948
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Overview
The Factories Act 1948 is the primary central legislation governing the working conditions of workers employed
in factories across India. It was enacted to consolidate and amend the law regulating labour in factories, with the
aim of ensuring the health, safety, welfare, and proper working conditions of factory workers. The Act applies to
premises employing 10 or more workers with power, or 20 or more workers without power. It is administered by
State Governments through Chief Inspectors of Factories. Amendments have been made over the years,
notably in 1976 and 1987, to strengthen protections.

Definition: Factory (Section 2(m))
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Section 2(m)
Under Section 2(m), a 'factory' means any premises including the precincts thereof: (a) whereon ten or more
workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of which a
manufacturing process is being carried on with the aid of power, or is ordinarily so carried on; or (b) whereon
twenty or more workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any
part of which a manufacturing process is being carried on without the aid of power, or is ordinarily so carried on.
The term does not include a mine, a mobile unit of the armed forces, a railway running shed, or a hotel,
restaurant or eating place.

Definition: Worker and Manufacturing Process (Section 2)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Section 2(l) and 2(k)
Section 2(l) defines a 'worker' as a person employed, directly or by or through any agency (including a
contractor), with or without the knowledge of the principal employer, whether for remuneration or not, in any
manufacturing process, or in cleaning any part of the machinery or premises used for a manufacturing process,
or in any other kind of work incidental to, or connected with, the manufacturing process. Section 2(k) defines
'manufacturing process' broadly to include making, altering, repairing, ornamenting, finishing, packing, oiling,
washing, cleaning, breaking up, demolishing or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a
view to its use, sale, transport, delivery, or disposal.

Working Hours – Adults: Maximum Daily and Weekly Hours (Sections
51, 54)

Source: Factories Act 1948 – Sections 51 and 54
Section 51 provides that no adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in a factory for more than
forty-eight hours in any week. Section 54 provides that no adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in a
factory for more than nine hours in any day. However, subject to the provisions of Section 51, a worker may be
required to work for more than nine hours in a day if the total number of hours worked does not exceed 48 in the
week. Where a worker works for more than nine hours on any day or more than 48 hours in any week, he is
entitled to overtime wages at twice the ordinary rate of wages (Section 59).

Overtime Wages (Section 59)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Section 59
Section 59 provides that where a worker works in a factory for more than nine hours in any day or for more than
forty-eight hours in any week, he shall, in respect of overtime work, be entitled to wages at the rate of twice his
ordinary rate of wages. 'Ordinary rate of wages' means the basic wages plus such allowances, including the
cash equivalent of the advantage accruing through the concessional sale to workers of foodgrains and other
articles, as the worker is for the time being entitled to, but does not include a bonus and wages for overtime
work. Claims for overtime wages can be made before the Labour Commissioner or appropriate authority.

Spread-Over and Rest Intervals (Sections 55, 56)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Sections 55 and 56
Section 55 provides that the periods of work of adult workers in a factory each day shall be so fixed that no
period shall exceed five hours, and that no worker shall work for more than five hours before he has had an
interval for rest of at least half an hour. Section 56 states that the spread-over of work, including rest intervals,
shall not exceed ten and a half hours in any day. The Chief Inspector may, in certain circumstances, increase
the spread-over up to twelve hours. Any violation of these provisions makes the employer liable for penalties
under Section 92.

Weekly Rest Day (Section 52)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Section 52
Section 52 provides that no adult worker shall be required or allowed to work in a factory on the first day of the
week (i.e., Sunday), unless: (a) he has or will have a holiday for a whole day on one of the three days
immediately before or after the said day; and (b) the manager of the factory has, before the said day or the
substituted day (whichever is earlier), delivered a notice at the office of the Inspector specifying the day which is
to be substituted. A worker is entitled to a paid weekly day off and cannot be made to work seven days in a row
without a compensatory day off.

Annual Leave with Wages (Section 79) — KEY SECTION
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Section 79
Section 79 is the key provision on annual earned leave. Every worker who has worked for a period of 240 days
or more in a factory during a calendar year shall be allowed during the subsequent calendar year, leave with
wages for a number of days calculated as follows: (a) if an adult — one day for every twenty days of work
performed by him during the previous calendar year; (b) if a child — one day for every fifteen days of work
performed by him during the previous calendar year. A worker may accumulate earned leave up to 30 days for
adults (45 for children). If a worker is discharged or dismissed or quits, he is entitled to wages in lieu of
unavailed leave. Leave cannot be denied arbitrarily; the employer must grant it within the first half of the
calendar year unless a worker requests otherwise.

Sick Leave and Casual Leave (State Rules)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Leave Rules (State-Specific)
The Factories Act 1948 itself does not prescribe a specific number of sick leave days at the central level; this is
governed by the rules framed by each State Government under the Act. Most State Factory Rules provide for:
(a) Casual Leave — typically 8 to 10 days per year, non-accumulative, for sudden or urgent personal matters;
(b) Sick Leave — typically 7 to 14 days per year, which may or may not require a medical certificate. In
Maharashtra, the Maharashtra Factories Rules 1963 apply. Under these rules, workers are also entitled to
protections under the Employees' State Insurance Act 1948 if the factory is covered under ESI, which provides
sickness benefit for up to 91 days per benefit period for insured workers.

ESI Sickness Benefit (Employees' State Insurance Act 1948 – Key
Provisions)
Source: Employees' State Insurance Act 1948 – Sickness Benefit
Under the Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act 1948, an insured worker is entitled to sickness benefit in the
form of periodical cash payments for periods of certified sickness. Sickness benefit is available for a maximum
of 91 days in two consecutive benefit periods. The daily rate is approximately 70% of average daily wages. To
claim sickness benefit, the insured person must: (1) have paid contributions for at least 78 days in the
corresponding contribution period; (2) obtain a certificate of sickness from an appointed ESI doctor; (3) remain
under medical care. Extended sickness benefit for specified long-term diseases can extend up to 2 years. The
employer cannot dismiss a worker during the period she/he is receiving ESI sickness benefit.

Health Provisions: Cleanliness, Ventilation, Lighting (Sections 11–20)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Chapter III (Sections 11–20)
Chapter III of the Factories Act mandates minimum health standards. Section 11 requires every factory to be
kept clean and free from effluvia arising from any drain, privy or other nuisance. Section 13 requires adequate

ventilation by circulation of fresh air, and maintenance of a reasonable temperature. Section 14 requires all
practicable measures to be taken to prevent dust and fume inhalation. Section 16 requires all inside walls,
partitions and ceilings to be whitewashed or colour-washed at least once in 14 months, or painted at least once
every 5 years. Section 17 mandates sufficient and suitable lighting, natural or artificial, in every part of the
factory where workers are working or passing.

Welfare Provisions: Canteen, Rest Rooms, Crèches (Sections 42–50)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Chapter V (Sections 42–50)
Chapter V covers welfare measures. Section 42 requires adequate washing facilities. Section 43 requires
facilities for storing and drying clothing. Section 44 requires sitting facilities for workers who are obliged to work
standing. Section 45 requires first-aid boxes or cupboards — at least one per 150 workers — staffed by a
trained person. Section 46: where more than 250 workers are ordinarily employed, the occupier must provide a
canteen. Section 47: where 150 or more workers are ordinarily employed, suitable rest rooms or lunch rooms
must be provided. Section 48: where 30 or more women workers are ordinarily employed, a crèche (room for
children under 6 years) must be maintained.

Safety Provisions: Fencing of Machinery, Prohibition of Employment
near Dangerous Machinery (Sections 21–41)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Chapter IV (Sections 21–41)
Chapter IV deals with safety measures. Section 21 requires every dangerous part of any machinery to be
securely fenced. Section 22 restricts work on or near machinery in motion to trained adult males wearing tight
clothing. Section 23 prohibits employment of young persons on dangerous machines unless trained and
supervised. Section 27 prohibits employment of women and children near cotton-openers. Section 28 requires
hoists and lifts to be of good mechanical construction, sound material, and adequate strength. Section 36 deals
with precautions against dangerous fumes, gases and dust. Section 38 requires every factory to have adequate
fire-fighting equipment and means of escape in case of fire. Violation of safety provisions can attract penalties
under Section 92.

Employment of Women Workers (Sections 19, 22, 27, 66)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Women Workers Provisions
The Factories Act contains specific protections for women: Section 19 requires separate toilet facilities for
women. Section 22 restricts women from working on or near dangerous machinery in motion. Section 27
prohibits employment of women near cotton-openers. Section 66 is crucial — it prohibits employment of women
in any factory except between the hours of 6 AM and 7 PM. State Governments may modify this (allowing night
shifts up to 10 PM or even beyond), but adequate safeguards including transportation, security, and written
consent of the woman worker must be ensured. Night work amendments were made in several states including
Maharashtra. The Maternity Benefit Act 1961 provides additional protections.

Employment of Young Persons and Children (Sections 67–77)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Chapter VII: Young Persons
Chapter VII governs employment of young persons. Section 67 prohibits employment of children below 14 years
in any factory. Section 68: children between 14 and 15 years may only work with a certificate of fitness granted
by a certifying surgeon, and only for 4.5 hours per day, and only during the day (not at night). Section 71
prohibits employment of a child for more than four and a half hours on any day and during any night. Section 72:
all certificates of fitness must be kept readily available. Section 77 defines 'adolescent' as a person who has
completed 15 but not 18 years, and 'child' as under 15. Young persons (adolescents) are entitled to all leave,
wages, and welfare provisions under the Act.

Duties of Occupier and Manager (Sections 7A, 7B, 11–20)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Sections 7A and 7B
Section 7A imposes a general duty on every occupier to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health,
safety and welfare of all workers while they are at work in the factory. This includes: (a) provision and
maintenance of plant and systems of work that are safe; (b) arrangements for safe use, handling, storage and
transport of articles and substances; (c) provision of information, instruction, training and supervision necessary
to ensure health and safety; (d) maintenance of the workplace in a condition that is safe; (e) provision and
maintenance of a working environment that is safe. Section 7B imposes similar duties on manufacturers to
ensure safety of articles designed or manufactured for use in factories. The occupier must file a written
statement of policy with respect to the health and safety of workers.

Prohibition of Arbitrary Dismissal During Leave / ESI Period
Source: Factories Act 1948 & ESI Act – Protection Against Dismissal
The Factories Act does not explicitly prohibit dismissal during sick leave, but combined with other laws, strong
protections exist. Under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947, a workman (worker in an industrial establishment)
cannot be dismissed without following due procedure — notice, inquiry, and approval of appropriate authority for
establishments with 100+ workers (Section 25F, 25N). Under the ESI Act, it is unlawful for an employer to
dismiss, discharge, or reduce in rank a worker during any period in which sickness benefit or maternity benefit is
being claimed or payable to the worker (Section 73, ESI Act). Any dismissal in violation is void and the worker is
entitled to reinstatement.

Notice of Accident and Dangerous Occurrences (Section 88)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Section 88

Section 88 requires the manager of a factory to send notice to the Inspector and such other authorities as
prescribed when any accident occurs in the factory which causes death or injury preventing a worker from
working for a period of 48 hours or more. Notice must be sent within the prescribed time. Section 88A requires
similar reporting for dangerous occurrences (explosions, fire, collapse of structure, release of gases, etc.) even
if no injury occurs. Section 89 requires reporting of notifiable diseases (as listed in the Third Schedule) by the
factory manager to the Inspector of Factories. Failure to report is an offence under Section 92.

Penalties for Violations (Sections 92–106)
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Chapter X: Penalties and Procedure
Section 92 is the principal penalty provision. If there is a contravention of any provision of the Act or the rules
made thereunder, the occupier and manager of the factory shall each be guilty of an offence and punishable
with imprisonment for up to 2 years, or a fine up to Rs 1,00,000, or both. If the contravention continues after
conviction, a further fine of up to Rs 1,000 per day may be levied. Section 94 provides that where the
contravention is by a worker, he may be fined up to Rs 500. Section 96A provides enhanced penalties for
contravention of provisions relating to hazardous processes — imprisonment up to 7 years extendable to 10
years if the failure to comply results in death of or serious bodily injury to any person.

Key Case Laws Under the Factories Act
Source: Factories Act 1948 – Important Case Laws
1. Workmen of Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. v. Management (1973 SC): The Supreme Court held that overtime
wages under Section 59 must be calculated on the basis of basic wage plus dearness allowance and other
regular allowances, not just basic wage. 2. Rohtas Industries Ltd. v. Rohtas Industries Staff Union (1976 SC):
Clarified that the definition of 'worker' under Section 2(l) includes contract workers deployed at a factory. 3. State
of Maharashtra v. Sayyed Ismail (1965 Bom HC): Held that even a single day's violation of working hour limits is
punishable under Section 92. 4. Hindustan Lever Ltd. v. Workmen (1984 SC): Held that earned leave
encashment on termination is a statutory right under Section 79 and cannot be waived. 5. On denial of leave:
Courts have consistently held that earned leave under Section 79 is a statutory entitlement and employers
cannot arbitrarily deny it; denial without valid reason can be challenged before the Labour Commissioner.

Section 4:
Minimum rate of wages.
(1) Any minimum rate of wages fixed or revised by the appropriate Government in respect of scheduled employments under section 3 may consist of- (i) a basic rate of wages and a special allowance at a rate to be adjusted, at such intervals and in such manner as the appropriate Government may direct, to accord as nearly as practicable with the variation in the cost of living index number applicable to such workers (hereinafter referred to as the "cost of living allowance"); or (ii) a basic rate of wages with or without the cost of living allowance, and the cash value of the concessions in respect of supplies of essential commodities at concessional rates, where so authorized; or (iii) an all-inclusive rate allowing for the basic rate, the cost of living allowance and the cash value of the concessions, if any.

Section 22C:
Offences by companies.
(1) If the person committing any offence under this Act is a company, every person who at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly:
Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such person liable to any punishment provided in this Act if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where an offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any, director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.
Explanation.-For the purposes of this section,- (a) "company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals, and (b) "director" in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm.

Where an employer is charged with an offence against this Act, he shall be entitled, upon complaint duly made by him, to have any other person whom he charges as the actual offender, brought before the Court at the time appointed for hearing the charge; and if, after the commission of the offence has been proved, the employer proves to the Satisfaction of the Court - (a) that he has used due diligence to enforce the execution of this Act, and (b) that the said other person committed the offence in question without his knowledge, consent or connivance, that other person shall be convicted of the offence and shall be liable to, the like punishment as if he were the employer and the employer shall be discharged:

Title: POSH Act Overview and Purpose
Keywords: POSH Act, Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace, prevention, prohibition, redressal, 2013
The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, commonly known
as the POSH Act, is a landmark Indian legislation enacted to protect women from sexual harassment at the workplace.
The Act came into force on 9 December 2013. It gives effect to the guidelines laid down by the Supreme Court of India
in Vishaka and Others v. State of Rajasthan (1997), which recognized sexual harassment at the workplace as a
violation of fundamental rights under Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution of India. The primary objectives of the
Act are: (1) prevention of sexual harassment of women at the workplace; (2) prohibition of all forms of sexual
harassment; (3) redressal of complaints of sexual harassment through a time-bound mechanism. The Act applies to all
workplaces — organized and unorganized sectors — across India, including government bodies, private companies,
NGOs, hospitals, educational institutions, sports institutions, and domestic workers' settings.

pageContent:
Title: Definition of Sexual Harassment under POSH Act
Keywords: definition, sexual harassment, unwelcome acts, physical contact, advances, demand, favours, sexually
coloured remarks
Under Section 2(n) of the POSH Act, 'sexual harassment' includes any one or more of the following unwelcome acts or
behaviour (whether directly or by implication): (a) physical contact and advances; (b) a demand or request for sexual
favours; (c) making sexually coloured remarks; (d) showing pornography; (e) any other unwelcome physical, verbal or
non-verbal conduct of sexual nature. Additionally, Section 3(2) specifies that the following circumstances, if they occur
or are present in relation to or connected with any act or behaviour of sexual harassment, may amount to sexual
harassment: (i) implied or explicit promise of preferential treatment in employment; (ii) implied or explicit threat of
detrimental treatment in employment; (iii) implied or explicit threat about present or future employment status; (iv)
interference with work or creating an intimidating, offensive or hostile work environment; (v) humiliating treatment likely
to affect the lady employee's health or safety. Any single incident meeting the above criteria constitutes sexual
harassment under the Act.

Title: Definition of Workplace and Aggrieved Woman
Keywords: workplace definition, aggrieved woman, employee, domestic worker, extended workplace, unorganized
sector
Under Section 2(o) of the POSH Act, 'workplace' includes: (i) any department, organisation, undertaking,
establishment, enterprise, institution, office, branch or unit established, owned, controlled or wholly or substantially
financed by funds provided by the government; (ii) any private sector organisation or a private venture, undertaking,
enterprise, institution, establishment, society, trust, non-governmental organisation, unit or service provider carrying on
commercial, professional, vocational, educational, entertainment, industrial, health services or financial activities
including production, supply, sale, distribution or service; (iii) hospitals or nursing homes; (iv) any sports institute,
stadium, sports complex or competition or games venue; (v) any place visited by the employee arising out of or during
the course of employment, including transportation provided by the employer; (vi) a dwelling place or a house. Under
Section 2(a), 'aggrieved woman' means in relation to a workplace, a woman of any age whether employed or not, who
alleges to have been subjected to any act of sexual harassment by the respondent. The definition specifically includes
women employed in the unorganized sector, domestic workers, and contract/temporary workers.

Title: Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) — Constitution
Keywords: Internal Complaints Committee, ICC, constitution, Presiding Officer, members, employer, organisation with
10 or more employees

Section 4 of the POSH Act mandates that every employer of a workplace employing 10 or more employees shall
constitute an Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) at each office or branch. The ICC shall consist of: (a) a Presiding
Officer who shall be a woman employed at a senior level at the workplace from amongst the employees. If a
senior-level woman employee is not available, the Presiding Officer shall be nominated from other offices or
administrative units of the workplace. If such a person is not available, the employer shall request the District Officer to
nominate a Presiding Officer from any other workplace; (b) not less than two members from amongst the employees
preferably committed to the cause of women or who have had experience in social work or have legal knowledge; (c)
one member from amongst non-governmental organisations or associations committed to the cause of women or a
person familiar with issues relating to sexual harassment. At least one-half of the total members of the ICC shall be
women. The Presiding Officer and every member of the ICC shall hold office for a period not exceeding three years
from the date of their nomination. The employer shall pay to the Presiding Officer and members such fees or
allowances as may be prescribed. Any member of the ICC can be removed from the ICC if they have been convicted
of an offence, found guilty of any disciplinary proceeding, or abused their position.

Title: Local Complaints Committee (LCC) — Constitution and Jurisdiction
Keywords: Local Complaints Committee, LCC, District Officer, unorganized sector, less than 10 employees, domestic
worker
Section 6 of the POSH Act requires the District Officer (appointed by the appropriate government) to constitute a Local
Complaints Committee (LCC) in each district to receive complaints of sexual harassment from establishments where
the ICC has not been constituted due to having fewer than 10 workers, or if the complaint is against the employer
himself, or if the aggrieved woman is a domestic worker. The LCC shall consist of: (a) a Chairperson to be nominated
from amongst the eminent women in the field of social work committed to the cause of women; (b) one member to be
nominated from amongst the women working in block, taluka, tehsil, ward or municipality in the district; (c) two
members, of whom at least one shall be a woman, to be nominated from NGOs or associations committed to the
cause of women or a person familiar with issues relating to sexual harassment — preferably one of these members
shall be from the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes or the minority community. The Chairperson and the
members of the LCC shall hold office for a period not exceeding three years. The jurisdiction of the LCC extends to the
entire district. The LCC has the same powers as the ICC for the purposes of holding an inquiry.

Title: Filing a Complaint — Process and Timeline
Keywords: complaint, filing, written complaint, six weeks, three months, incapacity, conciliation, aggrieved woman
Section 9 of the POSH Act governs the manner of filing a complaint. The aggrieved woman is required to make a
written complaint of sexual harassment to the ICC or LCC within three months from the date of the incident. In case of
a series of incidents, the complaint shall be filed within three months from the date of the last incident. Where the
aggrieved woman is unable to make a complaint on account of her physical or mental incapacity or death or otherwise,
her legal heir or any other prescribed person may make the complaint. If the aggrieved woman is unable to write, the
Presiding Officer or any member of the ICC or LCC shall render all reasonable assistance to the woman to make the
complaint in writing. The ICC or LCC, for reasons to be recorded in writing, may extend the time limit for filing the
complaint by another three months if it is satisfied that circumstances existed which prevented the woman from filing
the complaint within the original period. The complaint shall be made in writing to the ICC or LCC. The ICC or LCC
shall provide copies of the complaint to the respondent within seven working days of receiving the complaint.

Title: Conciliation Process
Keywords: conciliation, settlement, Section 10, ICC, LCC, no monetary settlement, before inquiry

Section 10 of the POSH Act provides for an optional conciliation mechanism before a formal inquiry is initiated. The
ICC or LCC, as the case may be, at the request of the aggrieved woman, may take steps to settle the matter between
her and the respondent through conciliation. Important restrictions under Section 10: (a) No monetary settlement shall
be made as the basis of conciliation. The Act explicitly prohibits cash-based resolution of sexual harassment
complaints at the conciliation stage. (b) Conciliation is initiated only at the request of the aggrieved woman — it cannot
be imposed on her. If conciliation is agreed to and a settlement is arrived at, the ICC or LCC shall record the
settlement and provide copies to both parties. No further inquiry shall be conducted once the matter is settled through
conciliation. If the aggrieved woman informs the ICC or LCC that any term or condition of the settlement has not been
complied with by the respondent, the ICC or LCC shall proceed to make an inquiry into the complaint as if no
settlement was arrived at, or forward the complaint to the police. Conciliation proceedings are confidential and no
document, communication or evidence produced shall be used in any subsequent inquiry.

Title: Inquiry Process — Procedure and Timeline
Keywords: inquiry, Section 11, natural justice, sixty days, opportunity of hearing, evidence, witnesses, inquiry report
Section 11 of the POSH Act sets out the procedure for conducting an inquiry into complaints of sexual harassment.
Where the aggrieved woman does not opt for conciliation or the conciliation fails, the ICC or LCC shall proceed to
make an inquiry. Key procedural requirements: (1) The inquiry shall be completed within a period of sixty days. (2)
Principles of natural justice must be followed — both the aggrieved woman and the respondent shall be given an
opportunity to be heard. (3) The respondent shall receive a copy of the complaint and shall submit a written reply with
supporting documents and the names and addresses of witnesses within ten working days from receipt of the
complaint. (4) The ICC or LCC shall have the same powers as a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 in
respect of: (a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining them on oath; (b) requiring the
discovery and production of documents; (c) any other matter which may be prescribed. (5) Parties shall not be allowed
to bring any legal practitioner to represent them before the ICC or LCC. (6) At the request of both parties, the inquiry
may be conducted at a neutral venue. (7) The inquiry proceedings shall be kept confidential. The ICC or LCC shall
have regard to the evidence adduced and submit the inquiry report within ten days from the completion of the inquiry
to the employer and the District Officer, as the case may be.

Title: Interim Relief During Inquiry
Keywords: interim relief, Section 12, transfer, leave, protection, restraint, pending inquiry
Section 12 of the POSH Act empowers the ICC or LCC to recommend interim measures during the pendency of an
inquiry. During the pendency of an inquiry, on a written request made by the aggrieved woman, the ICC or LCC may
recommend to the employer to: (a) transfer the aggrieved woman or the respondent to any other workplace; (b) grant
leave to the aggrieved woman up to a period of three months. This leave shall be in addition to the leave she would
otherwise be entitled to; (c) grant such other relief to the aggrieved woman as may be prescribed. The employer shall
implement the recommendations of the ICC or LCC and send a report of such implementation to it. This provision is
critical because it ensures that the aggrieved woman does not have to continue working alongside the respondent
during the inquiry, and protects her from further harassment or intimidation. The interim relief does not prejudice the
final outcome of the inquiry.

Title: Action on Inquiry Report — Penalties and Recommendations
Keywords: inquiry report, Section 13, action on findings, punishment, misconduct, deduction from salary, termination,
service rules

Section 13 of the POSH Act governs the action to be taken upon receipt of the inquiry report. If the ICC or LCC
concludes that the allegation against the respondent has been proved, it shall recommend to the employer or the
District Officer, as the case may be: (a) to take action for sexual harassment as a misconduct in accordance with the
provisions of the service rules applicable to the respondent, or where no such service rules exist, in such manner as
may be prescribed; (b) to deduct from the salary or wages of the respondent such sum as it may consider appropriate
to be paid to the aggrieved woman or to her legal heirs. The sum to be deducted shall be determined based on: (i) the
mental trauma, pain, suffering and emotional distress caused to the aggrieved woman; (ii) the loss in career
opportunity due to the incident of sexual harassment; (iii) medical expenses incurred by the victim for physical or
psychiatric treatment; (iv) the income and financial status of the respondent; (v) feasibility of such payment in lump
sum or in instalments. If the respondent fails to pay the sum deducted, the ICC or LCC may forward the order for
recovery of the sum as an arrear of land revenue. Where the employer is unable to make deductions from the salary
due to the respondent being no longer in service, the employer shall recover the sum as prescribed. The employer
shall act on the recommendations within sixty days of receipt of the inquiry report.

Title: Punishment for False or Malicious Complaints
Keywords: false complaint, malicious complaint, Section 14, punishment, not proved, action against complainant
Section 14 of the POSH Act provides for action in case of false or malicious complaints. Where the ICC or LCC arrives
at a conclusion that the allegation against the respondent is false or malicious, or the aggrieved woman or any other
person making the complaint has produced any forged or misleading document, it may recommend to the employer or
District Officer to take action against the woman or the person who made the complaint, in accordance with the service
rules. Important distinction under the Act: The mere inability to substantiate a complaint or provide adequate proof
does not attract penal action against the complainant. A complaint will be treated as false or malicious only if there is
clear and convincing evidence of deliberate falsehood, forgery, or malicious intent. The protection against false
complaints is meant to deter abuse of the grievance mechanism, but it should not be used to deter genuine
complainants from coming forward. The ICC or LCC must exercise this power with caution and must not penalise a
complainant simply because the inquiry finds the complaint not proved. Any action taken against a complainant under
this section must be proportionate and in accordance with the applicable service rules.

Title: Duties and Obligations of the Employer
Keywords: employer duties, Section 19, awareness, sensitisation, training, Internal Complaints Committee, display,
annual report
Section 19 of the POSH Act enumerates the duties and obligations of every employer. Every employer shall: (a)
provide a safe working environment at the workplace, including safety from all persons coming into contact at the
workplace; (b) display at any conspicuous place in the workplace the penal consequences of sexual harassment and
the order constituting the ICC; (c) organise workshops and awareness programmes at regular intervals for sensitising
the employees with the provisions of the Act and orientation programmes for the members of the ICC; (d) provide
necessary facilities to the ICC or LCC for dealing with the complaint and conducting an inquiry; (e) assist in securing
the attendance of the respondent and witnesses before the ICC or LCC; (f) make available such information to the ICC
or LCC as it may require having regard to the complaint made under sub-section (1) of Section 9; (g) cause to initiate
action under the IPC (Indian Penal Code) or any other law for the time being in force against the perpetrator if the
aggrieved woman so desires, or where the ICC or LCC determines that the circumstances of the case warrant such
action; (h) treat sexual harassment as a misconduct under the service rules and initiate action for such misconduct; (i)
monitor the timely submission of reports by the ICC. Additionally, employers must file an annual report with the District
Officer containing details of the number of complaints received, disposed of, and pending for more than 90 days.

Title: Appeal against Findings of ICC or LCC
Keywords: appeal, Section 18, court, tribunal, sixty days, aggrieved, recommendations not complied
Section 18 of the POSH Act provides a right to appeal to any person aggrieved by the recommendations made or
non-implementation of the recommendations by the ICC or LCC. Any person aggrieved by the findings or
recommendations made under Section 13 (action on inquiry report), or non-implementation of such recommendations
under Section 13 or 14, may prefer an appeal to the appropriate court or tribunal in accordance with the service rules
applicable to the said person. Where no service rules exist, the appeal shall lie to the court or tribunal as specified.
The appeal must be filed within sixty days of the recommendations. Important notes: (1) The right to appeal is
available to both the aggrieved woman and the respondent. (2) The court or tribunal hearing the appeal shall have the
power to confirm, modify or set aside the recommendations or orders appealed against. (3) The filing of an appeal
shall not affect any action already taken or recommended unless the court or tribunal directs otherwise. (4) Where the
employer fails to implement the recommendations, the aggrieved woman can also approach the court or tribunal for
enforcement.

Title: Penalty for Non-Compliance by Employer
Keywords: penalty, employer non-compliance, Section 26, fine, cancellation of registration, licence, repeat offence
Section 26 of the POSH Act prescribes penalties for employers who fail to comply with the provisions of the Act. Any
employer who fails to: (a) constitute an ICC; (b) take action on the recommendations of the ICC or LCC; (c) file the
annual report; or (d) comply with any other obligation under the Act — shall be punishable with a fine which may
extend to Rs. 50,000. In case of a second or subsequent conviction, the fine shall be double the penalty that can be
imposed for the first offence. If the employer is a company, the government authority may also cancel or withdraw the
registration, licence or approval granted to the employer for carrying on their business or activity. The appropriate
government is empowered to impose higher penalties if the employer repeatedly violates the provisions. The penalties
under this section are in addition to any other penalty to which the employer may be liable under any other law for the
time being in force. Non-constitution of the ICC is a continuing offence and each day of default constitutes a separate
offence.

Title: Confidentiality Obligations under POSH Act
Keywords: confidentiality, Section 16, identity, respondent, aggrieved woman, witnesses, disclosure, penalty
Section 16 of the POSH Act imposes strict confidentiality obligations regarding the contents of the complaint, inquiry
proceedings, recommendations, and actions taken. The ICC or LCC and the employer shall not publish, communicate,
or make known to the public, press, or media in any manner the contents of the complaint made under the Act.
Specifically: (a) the identity of the aggrieved woman; (b) the identity of the respondent; (c) the identity of the witnesses;
(d) any information relating to conciliation and inquiry proceedings; (e) recommendations of the ICC, LCC or employer;
(f) action taken by the employer under the Act — shall not be disclosed. Section 17 provides that any person who
contravenes the confidentiality provisions shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed in the service rules or, where no
service rules exist, shall be liable to a fine of Rs. 5,000. The confidentiality obligation does not prevent the disclosure
of information for the purpose of taking action under the Act. Victims who wish to speak publicly about their
experiences may do so but the ICC, LCC, and employer remain bound by confidentiality even if the aggrieved woman
consents to disclosure.

Title: Protection against Retaliation and Victimisation
Keywords: retaliation, victimisation, protection, adverse action, unfair dismissal, demotion, threats after complaint

The POSH Act, read with the duties of employers under Section 19, provides protection against retaliation and
victimisation of complainants. An employer is prohibited from taking any adverse employment action against an
aggrieved woman or a witness who has made a complaint or deposed before the ICC or LCC. Adverse actions that
are prohibited include: (a) termination of employment; (b) demotion; (c) denial of promotion or increments; (d) transfer
to an undesirable location; (e) harassment or intimidation; (f) any other detrimental treatment in employment. If the
aggrieved woman or a witness is subjected to retaliatory action, the same shall be treated as a fresh instance of
misconduct and the employer shall be required to take action accordingly. A separate complaint may be filed regarding
the retaliatory action before the ICC or LCC. The provisions relating to interim relief under Section 12 can also be
invoked to protect the aggrieved woman from retaliatory treatment during the pendency of an inquiry. Courts and
tribunals have consistently held that retaliation against a POSH complainant amounts to a hostile work environment
and can attract separate liability under both the POSH Act and general employment law.

Title: ICC Inquiry Report — Format and Submission
Keywords: inquiry report, Section 13, ten days, findings, recommendations, employer, District Officer, submission
format
Upon completion of the inquiry, the ICC or LCC is required to submit a detailed inquiry report. The inquiry report must
be submitted within ten days from the completion of the inquiry, to: (a) the employer, in the case of an inquiry by the
ICC; (b) the District Officer, in the case of an inquiry by the LCC. The inquiry report shall contain: (1) a brief description
of the complaint and the allegations; (2) a summary of the evidence adduced by both parties; (3) findings of fact; (4)
findings on the applicability of the POSH Act to the facts; (5) a finding on whether the allegation has been proved or
not proved; (6) if proved, recommendations regarding action to be taken under the service rules or monetary
deduction; (7) if not proved, whether any false complaint or forgery is established and if so, recommendations
regarding action against the complainant. The employer is required to act on the recommendations within sixty days of
receipt of the inquiry report. The employer shall notify both parties of the action taken within sixty days. A copy of the
report shall be made available to the concerned parties. Where the employer does not take action within sixty days,
the aggrieved woman can file an appeal under Section 18.

Title: Annual Report and Monitoring
Keywords: annual report, District Officer, Section 21, number of complaints, pending cases, awareness training,
monitoring
Section 21 of the POSH Act mandates that the ICC shall prepare an annual report and submit it to the employer and
the District Officer at the end of each calendar year. The annual report must include: (a) number of complaints of
sexual harassment received in the year; (b) number of complaints disposed of during the year; (c) number of cases
pending for more than ninety days; (d) number of workshops or awareness programmes against sexual harassment
carried out; (e) nature of action taken by the employer or District Officer. The employer, in turn, is required to include in
its annual report the number of cases filed under the Act and their disposal. Similarly, the appropriate government
shall compile the data from all District Officers and prepare a report on the status of implementation of the Act for
submission to the Central Government. This monitoring mechanism ensures accountability at every level — from the
employer to the District Officer to the State and Central Government. Failure to submit the annual report is treated as
non-compliance under Section 26 and may attract penalties.

Title: Special Provisions — Domestic Workers
Keywords: domestic worker, household, employer at home, LCC, complaint by domestic worker, unorganised sector
The POSH Act specifically extends protection to domestic workers employed in households. Under Section 2(a), an

'aggrieved woman' includes a domestic worker. Under Section 2(o), a 'workplace' includes a dwelling place or a
house. This means domestic workers can file complaints under the POSH Act even though they work in private
homes. Since domestic employers typically employ fewer than 10 people, they are not required to constitute an ICC.
Complaints by domestic workers must be filed before the Local Complaints Committee (LCC) of the district. The LCC
has the same powers as the ICC to conduct an inquiry. The employer (i.e., the person in whose household the
domestic worker is employed) is also covered under the employer obligations of the Act. The appropriate government
is empowered to specify additional measures for the protection of domestic workers. Courts have recognised the
vulnerability of domestic workers to sexual harassment given the isolated nature of their workplace, and have directed
employers and LCCs to be especially vigilant in such cases.

Title: Key Case Laws under POSH Act
Keywords: case law, Vishaka, Apparel Export, High Court, Supreme Court, ICC obligations, employer liability, judicial
interpretation
Key judicial decisions shaping the POSH Act framework: (1) Vishaka and Others v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 6 SCC
241 — The Supreme Court of India laid down mandatory guidelines for employers to prevent, prohibit, and redress
sexual harassment at the workplace. These guidelines became the legislative basis for the POSH Act 2013. (2)
Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999) 1 SCC 759 — The Supreme Court held that sexual
harassment need not involve physical contact and that any unwelcome sexual act short of molestation is actionable.
(3) Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) 1 SCC 311 — The Supreme Court directed all states and union
territories to strictly implement the Vishaka guidelines and mandated the setting up of complaints committees in all
workplaces. (4) High Court decisions have consistently held that: (a) the ICC has a duty to follow principles of natural
justice; (b) the employer cannot be merely a rubber stamp for ICC recommendations; (c) the definition of 'workplace' is
to be interpreted broadly to include off-site locations and events; (d) the three-month limitation for filing complaints can
be extended for good cause. (5) Courts have also held that even a single serious incident of sexual harassment is
sufficient to establish a hostile work environment.

9C. Setting up of Grievance Redressal Machinery.-(1) Every industrial establishment employing twenty or more workmen shall have one or more Grievance Redressal Committee for the resolution of disputes arising out of individual grievances.
(2) The Grievance Redressal Committee shall consist of equal number of members from the employer and the workmen.
(3) The chairperson of the Grievance Redressal Committee shall be selected from the employer and from among the workmen alternatively on rotation basis every year.

Submission.-(1) Any employer and a Representative Union or, in the absence of any registered Representative Union, any other Union which is representative of employees may, by a written agreement, agree to submit any present or future industrial dispute or class of such disputes to the arbitration of any person whether such arbitrator is named in such agreement or not. Proceedings in arbitration.-The proceedings in arbitration under this Chapter shall be in accordance with the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1940 (Central Act X of 1940) in so far as they are applicable and the powers which are exercisable by a Civil Court under the said provisions shall be exercisable by the Industrial Tribunal.

Dispute to be referred to Industrial Tribunal if no arbitrator appointed.-Notwithstanding anything contained in this Chapter, if no provision has been made in any submission for the appointment of an arbitrator or where by reason of any circumstances no arbitrator is appointed, such dispute may be referred by the State Government for adjudication by the Industrial Tribunal.

22. Prohibition of strikes and lock-outs.-(1) No person employed in a public utility service shall go on strike in breach of contract- (a) without giving to the employer notice of strike, as hereinafter provided, within six weeks before striking; or (b) within fourteen days of giving such notice; or (c) before the expiry of the date of strike specified in any such notice as aforesaid; or (d) during the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings.
(2) No employer carrying on any public utility service shall lock-out any of his workmen- (a) without giving them notice of lock-out as hereinafter provided, within six weeks before locking out; or (b) within fourteen days of giving such notice; or (c) before the expiry the date of lock-out specified in any such notice as aforesaid; or (d) during the pendency of any conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer and seven days after the conclusion of such proceedings.
(3) The notice of lock-out or strike under this section shall not be necessary where there is already in existence a strike or, as the case may be, lock-out in the public utility service, but the employer shall send intimation of such lock-out or strike on the day on which it is declared, to such authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government either generally or for a particular area or for a particular class of public utility services.
(4) The notice of strike referred to in sub-section (1) shall be given by such number of persons to such person or persons and in such manner as may be prescribed.
(5) The notice of lock-out referred to in sub-section (2) shall be given in such manner as may be prescribed.
(6) If on any day an employer receives from any persons employed by him any such notices as are referred to in sub-section (1) or gives to any persons employed by him any such notices as are referred to in sub-section (2), he shall within five days thereof report to the appropriate Government or to such authority as that Government may prescribe the number of such notices received or given on that day.
23. Introduction
The Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 is a social welfare legislation in India that provides a statutory
right to employees to receive gratuity as a retirement benefit for long and continuous service.
Applicability
The Act applies to factories, mines, oil fields, plantations, ports, railway companies, shops and
other establishments with 10 or more employees.
Eligibility
An employee becomes eligible for gratuity after completing at least 5 years of continuous service.
Exceptions exist in cases of death or disablement.
Definition of Gratuity
Gratuity is a lump sum payment made by an employer to an employee as a token of appreciation
for services rendered.
Calculation of Gratuity

Gratuity is a lump sum payment made by an employer to an employee as a token of appreciation

Calculation of Gratuity
Gratuity = (15/26) × Last Drawn Salary × Number of Completed Years of Service. Here, 26
represents working days in a month.
Payment Timeline
Gratuity must be paid within 30 days from the date it becomes payable.
Forfeiture
Gratuity may be partially or fully forfeited if an employee is terminated for misconduct involving
violence, moral turpitude, or damage to property.
Nomination
Employees are required to nominate family members to receive gratuity in case of death.

Conclusion
The Act ensures financial security for employees after retirement or termination, promoting social
